items.summary: Japan's two biggest property insurers reported sharp jumps in cyberinsurance claim activity for October, attributing the rise to increasingly sophisticated AI-fuelled attacks. Tokio Marine Holdings received three times the usual number of cyberclaim notifications that month, while Sompo Holdings said claims were running at 2½ times higher than its average over the year ending Sept 30, 2026; both figures came from earnings briefings on Nov 19. The surge raises payout risk even as incident counts fuel demand for coverage—Sompo reported that inquiries about raising limits or adding items tripled—and mirrors a global trend in which US insurers logged more than 56,000 cyberclaims in 2025, up 20% year on year. Tokio Marine's Yoshinari Endo said the rise would have some impact on full-year results but expects losses to stay within its initial annual plan and keep the business profitable through March 2027; Sompo's Junsuke Koike pointed to expansion room as only 8.8% of small- and medium-sized Japanese firms hold cyberinsurance, per a 2025 General Insurance Association survey. Insurers are responding by tightening underwriting—Tokio Marine may cap payouts or restrict terms—and offering prevention services, with Sompo launching a Trend Micro-backed vulnerability-monitoring service in December; standard payout limits run from about 100 million yen (S$812,000) to several hundred million yen per contract. The limitation is that these are claim-activity and inquiry metrics rather than confirmed losses or final earnings impact, so the financial exposure remains provisional.
items.title: AI-driven cyberattacks surge claims at Japan's largest insurers as Tokio Marine sees tripled October notifications and Sompo reports 2½ times higher activity than its trailing year.

items.summary: The episode list for 'Tech Now' presents a themed collection of technology-focused programs, anchored by an installment on the America's Cup that examines how sailing is evolving. The broader lineup spans AI applications—such as landslide early-warning systems and counterfeit detection—as well as innovations in healthcare (3D imaging in heart surgery), space exploration, gaming events like Gamescom and CES 2026, environmental monitoring of forests and rising seas, and sports technology across the World Cup, Winter Olympics, WWE, and Esports. The list conveys only episode titles and durations; it offers no specific claims about technical capabilities, performance figures, or outcomes for any featured innovation.
items.title: Tech Now: America's Cup and Other Tech-Driven Episodes

items.summary: A BBC test asked four AI models to find a 55-inch TV deal, but each produced unreliable results: ChatGPT's top pick was £499 down from £649 at Joybuy, yet both retailers said it was no longer listed; Claude recommended TCLs whose links went to dead pages or year-old round-ups; Gemini named correct prices for one model (£649) but a sold-out item and another priced £60 higher than Argos's £539; Alexa gave accurate Amazon-only prices, including its own Ember at £532. The models repeatedly surfaced the same brands—Hisense, TCL, Samsung—and offered no store links except Gemini, which named retailers without working connections. Tech journalist Alex Hughes reported that agentic AI mode saved time but still returned inconsistent live pricing; he bought one of seven ChatGPT suggestions later for a lower price in-store and said he probably wouldn't use AI again this year. Naureen Mohammed noted last year's prices were served up as today's deals when retailers fail to update them, with Amazon appearing in half her responses and Currys close behind, while Which?'s Hannah Walsh warned that inaccurate pricing wastes time checking options or misses better models within budget.
items.title: AI shopping tools gave inconsistent Black Friday TV deals

items.summary: Security researcher HD Moore planted exactly one unused secret—AWS access keys, SSH passwords, DNS names, and private git repository references—into a single prompt routed through each provider in a network of widely used AI services. The secrets were never previously used, and Moore controlled the infrastructure receiving any requests using them, so if leaked they would identify which link exposed the data. He seeded 2 million canaries across brokers such as OpenRouter and Vercel to test whether sensitive information leaks through this chain of AI routers and how it is exploited when it does. The experiment found an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve, exposing security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations across the network.
items.title: Researcher's 2 million canaries reveal AI service networks leak sensitive data

items.summary: An update to METR's widely shared but often misinterpreted "time horizon" plot now incorporates harder, judgment-laden and open-ended tasks—such as designing new AI evaluations or scoring philosophical arguments—that the original suite omitted because they were difficult to verify. On these tasks, even though frontier models already outperform nearly everyone on software engineering, not a single AI-designed evaluation was judged useful by METR employees, and models also fell short of humans; OpenAI separately reported its models underperforming on real-world employee-assigned work versus the easier verifiable tasks in the original suite. The new plot still shows exponential progress—frontier models doubled the difficulty of completed tasks every four months—but completion times for many hard tasks are now estimates rather than measured, since paying people to attempt hundreds-of-hours or expert-only tasks is impractical, and few such tasks are included enough to project trends reliably; METR researchers acknowledge that clean trend extrapolation on these underspecified tasks remains unlikely. Experts like Sayash Kapoor welcome the shift toward open-ended evaluations as a necessary step but caution there is much more work before definitive answers about automated AI research and development emerge.
items.title: METR's updated AI time horizon plot adds hard-to-verify tasks where models still lag humans

items.summary: The International Energy Agency published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that it says is reshaping how countries think about energy security. The report finds the drive to cut dependence on imported fossil fuels—reinforced by the Strait of Hormuz crisis—is accelerating electrification and a shift toward domestic sources, including renewables, but warns electricity demand is surging, grids are struggling to keep pace, and energy-security concerns are extending coal's life in some countries while pursuing security alone won't deliver emissions cuts needed for climate goals. On COP31, the IEA projects that under current and proposed policies electricity will account for only 29% of final energy consumption by 2035—half the increase needed to reach the target of 35%. Nearly half of road-transport fossil fuel demand and more than a third of low- and medium-temperature industrial heat could be electrified at competitive cost today, but countries need detailed plans for transport, heating, and heavy industry plus transmission investment; Germany has cut manufacturer electricity taxes and subsidized grid charges. Cooling is projected to overtake building-heating demand globally for the first time by 2035, with cooling forecast to grow about 70% more than data-center demand that year even as it accounts for only 12% of global electricity consumption under current policies but could reach around 30% during peak periods. Oil demand is expected to level off by 2030—China's EV-driven slowdown continuing while India still rises—and coal use in 2035 is now projected higher than a year ago, though global coal demand falls 14% between 2025 and 2035 as power generation declines more sharply than industrial use (which falls just 5%). The IEA estimates about 400 billion cubic meters of new LNG export capacity could come online by 2035 yet exceed stated-policy demand by 70 bcm, risking underused infrastructure. Meeting electricity needs will require at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines plus another 15 million kilometers upgraded or replaced; since major grid projects take 5 to 15 years—far longer than many renewables—the IEA urges faster permitting and connections alongside storage, demand-response (as Brazil does), smart-grid controls, and distributed generation. The findings are attributed by CleanTechnica's Nick Wayth of the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition; all projections reflect current and proposed policies rather than outcomes.
items.title: IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026 says energy-security push is accelerating electrification but short of COP31 target, with cooling and coal as wildcards.

items.summary: The Department of Interior leased more than [q1: 31 million acres] of Pacific waters to a company seeking polymetallic nodules, marking the first time such a lease has been issued in U.S. waters; no commercial deep-sea mining operations have begun anywhere yet. Wetstone U.S. Ventures bid $6 million on two exploration areas adjacent to the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument and became provisional winner of Thursday's auction at Ventura County Fire Department, though actual mining would require further federal approvals beyond current mapping and surveying activities. The lease sale was contested: a federal judge in Hawaiʻi ruled days earlier that the Marine Minerals Administration violated the Endangered Species Act by not accounting for impacts on dozens of endangered species including whales, leatherback sea turtles, oceanic whitetip sharks and giant manta rays; Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton called it an unlawful act and vowed to push for voiding. The new office was established earlier this year within Interior to promote the Trump administration's agenda to secure critical minerals.
items.title: Trump administration issues first-ever U.S. deep-sea mining lease off American Samoa.

items.summary: BYD has previewed a camouflaged flagship people mover (MPV) under its Ocean lineup, with general manager Zhang Zhuo confirming it is “coming soon” but without a specific date. Local reports suggest an official debut next week at the 2026 Guangzhou Auto Show, which opens on November 27; this remains unconfirmed by BYD itself. The previewed vehicle resembles recent spy images and features a roof-mounted LiDAR and traditional pull-style door handles, though it does not closely resemble the futuristic Ocean-V concept shown earlier at the 2026 Beijing Auto Show. The Ocean MPV is expected to be “flagship-worthy” with premium tech such as zero-gravity seats and multiple digital screens, and its size should match that of the Xia minivan (5,145 mm long, 1,970 mm wide, 1,805 mm tall, 3,045 mm wheelbase). It is expected to use BYD’s latest-generation DM-i plug-in hybrid system with a 1.5L engine and a 200 kW electric motor. Pricing details have not been announced; the Ocean MPV would fill a gap between the Denza D9 (starting above 300,000 yuan) and the Xia (around 250,000 yuan / $37,500). All specifications are based on previews and reports rather than official confirmations.
items.title: BYD previews new flagship Ocean MPV ahead of expected Guangzhou Auto Show debut

items.summary: Moment Energy unveiled its Nova battery storage system at RE+ in Las Vegas, already in production at Megafactory 1 near Vancouver. Each unit delivers [q2: 500 kWh] of energy and [q3: 200 kW] of power with a footprint of [q4: 2.94 m] by [q5: 1.80 m], or [q6: 9.7 x] [q7: 5.9 ft]. The system can use packs from different EV models, and worn-out packs can be replaced without removing the enclosure or concrete pad; Moment says this service could keep a system in operation for more than 20 years. Nova claims to be the first storage system built from retired EV batteries to earn both UL [d1: 1973] certification for the batteries and UL [q8: 9540] certification for the complete system, with testing under UL [q9: 9540A], while its factory is certified under UL [d2: 1974]. It uses liquid cooling, detects smoke, heat, and flammable gases, and operates from −[q10: 13F] to [q11: 122F], or −[q12: 25C] to [q13: 50C]. Moment says an independent review found Nova meets US federal sourcing restrictions tied to the clean electricity investment tax credit. Orders are open, with first units expected to ship in Q1 [d3: 2027].
items.title: Moment Energy's Nova storage system repurposes retired EV batteries with modular pack replacement and safety certifications.

items.summary: The Trump administration's EPA formally appealed on Tuesday a federal judge's September ruling that the agency's termination of the low-income Solar for All program was illegal, even though a second judge also ruled in favor of protecting it. The program originated under the Inflation Reduction Act and had been envisioned as early as [d1: 2022], with EPA awarding grants to split a $7 billion pot by [d2: 2024] for community solar, rooftop solar, and battery storage across states, local governments, territories, tribes, and nonprofits. Advocates, installers, and a labor group challenged the August [d3: 2025] rollback in court; EPA never resumed grant handouts despite both rulings. Clean energy advocates argue the appeal contradicts administration promises to curb power prices, while six Republican Congress members urged Administrator Lee Zeldin to reinstate the program — though four of those signatories would be replaced by Democrats in the next Congress.
items.title: Trump EPA appealed a court ruling that had struck down its killing of Solar for All.

items.summary: Argentina is projecting a wave of dollar bond sales from its energy sector that will extend into the first half of [d2: 2027], according to Banco Santander. This week, major underwriter Banco Santander announced that a wave of dollar bond sales out of Argentina is projected to extend into the first half of [d2: 2027] as the nation's energy sector continues to go gangbusters. Bloomberg reported earlier this week that strong balance sheets and growing energy shipments have made blue-chip energy credits favorites among international investors, helping insulate them from bouts of volatility that have hit Argentine sovereign debt and weaker credits. Sales are expected to taper off slightly in [d3: 2027], but remain high; this year bond sales have already netted more than [q1: $11 billion] with the rest of [d4: 2026] still ahead, while next year's sales are expected to clock in at around [q2: $9 billion], according Mariano Urquiola, head of Corporate and Investment Banking at Santander Argentina. Experts expect a strong first two quarters as borrowers race to buy bonds before the October presidential election, which could potentially disrupt the national economy. The boom is driven primarily by Vaca Muerta shale production, having produced [q3: 670,000 barrels] of oil and [q4: 95 million cubic metres] of natural gas per day in August—[q5: 72 percent] of Argentina's total oil output and [q6: 62 percent] of its gas production. State-run YPF projects that by [d6: 2031] Vaca Muerta will generate [q7: $50 billion] in export dollars, potentially rivaling agriculture; the trade balance surplus has grown since [d7: 2022]. TotalEnergies announced a planned investment of [q8: $10 billion], with CEO Patrick Pouyanne targeting production enhancement to [q9: 16 million cubic metres] per day. The boom is also extending into energy storage, where CATL opened an Argentine commercial office after being pushed out of the United States by 'America First' policymaking.
items.title: Argentine energy firms are racing to sell dollar bonds before October's presidential election.

items.summary: Samsung rolled out its One UI 9.5 Beta program, available from [q7: 17] November across India plus Germany, South Korea, Poland, Britain, and the US. The update targets only three devices—Galaxy S26, Galaxy S26+, and Galaxy S26 Ultra—while older Galaxy S models, the Galaxy Z series, and the Galaxy S26 FE are not yet included. The beta introduces five changes: App Lock (securing selected apps with fingerprint or biometric recognition), improved camera controls including a new zoom bar for Pro and Pro Video modes, Samsung Health Mind Note, medication tracking within Samsung Health, and accessibility features such as floating shortcuts and hearing-aid volume control.
items.title: Samsung launched One UI 9.5 Beta for three Galaxy S26 models in six countries starting November 17.

items.summary: According to Google's own security blog (reported by an unverified Hindi source), the company created 'Mirror Dimension,' a fake internet of shopping sites, social platforms and banking dashboards used only to evaluate its Chrome Gemini-based browsing AI agents. The system relies on gVisor technology to run these look-alike pages in a sandboxed environment while showing normal-looking URLs and valid certificates so that the browser's security warnings stay silent; Google states hackers cannot use it because access is limited to its private test network, though this claim rests entirely on the company's description. The stated purpose is to measure how well Chrome's AI agents resist attacks such as prompt injection—where hidden instructions in text or images coax an agent into wrong actions—and no results have been disclosed: Google has not said how often its AI agents succeeded or failed during testing, nor does it report outcomes beyond the setup itself.
items.title: Google built Mirror Dimension to test Chrome's AI agents against cyberattacks, not as a public internet.

items.summary: Apollo Global Management and Goldman Sachs have priced a roughly $44 billion debt financing for SpaceX, which the firms describe as the largest AI-related chip financing ever arranged. Investor demand exceeded supply, allowing the transaction to be upsized from an earlier arrangement in which an affiliate of Apollo agreed to buy chips and server hardware with total principal payments of about $40 billion. The proceeds are expected to fund deployment of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin chips as SpaceX expands its terrestrial AI computing footprint. The package includes roughly $25.17 billion of senior secured A3 notes maturing in April 2033 at a yield of 8.259 per cent, about $4.4 billion of senior secured A2 notes maturing in April 2031 at 7.66 per cent, and roughly $2.564 billion of class B subordinated secured notes maturing in April 2033 at 8.36 per cent. Lease schedules are expected to begin when the GPUs arrive in the first half of 2027. BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and accounts advised by KKR provided anchor commitments.
items.title: Apollo and Goldman Sachs priced a roughly $44 billion debt package to finance SpaceX's acquisition of Nvidia GPUs.

items.summary: The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that Databricks is in early, still-ongoing talks to raise several billion dollars in a new round that would value the data and AI software company at about $225 billion, citing people familiar with the matter; terms could change. The report noted Databricks did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment, so these are unconfirmed reports rather than stated plans from the company. For context, in August Databricks said it had raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation, underscoring investor demand tied to the AI boom.
items.title: Databricks in early talks to raise funds at $225 billion valuation

visual.alt: Bar chart. intelligence software company 225,000,000,000 $; raised 5,000,000,000 $.

items.summary: Jamie Dimon, chief executive of JP Morgan, said at a London event that the bank would find ways to claw back from an increase in the UK surcharge on banks' balance sheets, which is set to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. He described the penalty as unfair and framed his response as setting an example for governments about trade-offs, saying the decision was 'more in sorrow than in anger.' JP Morgan employs 23,000 people in the UK and is expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase; how it will absorb that cost remains unclear. Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising bank taxes and suggested in May he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower at Canary Wharf, though sources told the Guardian those building plans were still proceeding as chancellor John Healey's October budget took effect.
items.title: JP Morgan boss vows to offset UK bank tax rise he calls unfair

items.summary: After months of negotiations, leaks and late-night talks, the UK and EU have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. The document is presented as an outline rather than a final deal; its contents are not detailed beyond this framing, so specific provisions cannot be confirmed from the source provided.
items.title: UK and EU agree a 12-page statement on post-Brexit relationship terms

items.summary: The source is an undated, unattributed note proposing topics to raise in a planned conversation with author and biographer Walter Isaacson. The event would partly celebrate the reissue of his book 'The Innovators: How a Group of Hackers, Geniuses, and Geeks Created the Digital Revolution' and also mark the launch of his new podcast titled 'The Builders.' No specific questions are offered; only these two occasions are named as context for what should be asked. The note contains no figures or dates to report.
items.title: Pre-event question suggestions for a Walter Isaacson conversation

items.summary: The UK's new agreement with the EU removes border bureaucracy for agrifood exports, yet supermarkets have welcomed it without committing to price cuts. Industry insiders privately say too many moving parts in the world economy, including an energy price shock from war in the Middle East, mean lower shopping bills remain more hope than certainty at this stage; the government and industry simply hope reduced costs are passed on to customers. The deal may recover some of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, though not all of it, and smaller exporters could return to the large EU market even as extra checks or costs might fall instead on non-EU food imports. Government assessment puts economic gain at £5bn through this deal, or 0.14% by 2040; bringing agreements on food, emissions and youth together is forecast to give an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year. This modest figure still matches all past post-Brexit trade deals combined for expected growth in the Treasury's own assessment, though most economists predict much bigger gains elsewhere would come with greater constitutional battles.
items.title: UK-EU food deal cuts red tape but does not guarantee lower prices or large economic gains

items.summary: The bipartisan college sports legislation faces intensifying friction between chambers, with no guarantee next year's Democratic Congress will prioritize it—several backers view this session as the last real opportunity. Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) told House Majority Leader Steve Scalise that changing the Senate-passed version would be a 'mistake,' while pushing leaders toward an up-or-down vote; Scalise says the House plans only very narrow changes and will be ready to act in December, though he flagged possible internal GOP opposition. Senate Majority Leader John Thune suggested the bill could clear via suspension requiring a two-thirds majority if needed, noting that without codification 'you're going to spend your next decade in court.' Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash) acknowledged time is of the essence while listening to House concerns; Thune also met Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti ahead of his meeting with Scalise and cited LSU's decision to play RJ Luis after his two-way NBA signing as evidence college sports' landscape has become absurd. The bill bars professional athletes from playing in college and establishes transfer portal restrictions, drawing support from President Donald Trump.
items.title: Senate and House clash over college sports bill as December deadline looms

items.summary: US President Donald Trump called for chip maker Nvidia to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang, whom he described as "a good man" who "made some bad decisions." Huang resigned last week after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said at a Friday (Nov 20) press event that "I would love to see him be back," citing his role in creating the Blackwell chips and noting he had spoken positively about Huang to China's President Xi Jinping during a summit earlier this week. This contradicted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who stated Trump had not discussed Huang with Xi at their meeting in Shenzhen. Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said on an earnings call that "the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Separately, Bessent emphasized the US must maintain its lead over China in AI, describing super intelligence labs as a shield against foreign exploitation and noting Trump and Xi agreed humans should always be involved in military decisions made by artificial intelligence. Huang has offered to return but was rejected by the board.
items.title: Trump urges Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang

items.summary: Technology shares nosedived globally after Anthropic's Nasdaq debut underperformed expectations, with the firm's price briefly rising from an initial offering of US$[q2: 83] to over US$[q3: 110] on Thursday but then falling back below US$[q4: 89] at Friday's close. The disappointing debut reinforced concerns about elevated AI valuations and the enormous capital commitments required for growth, according to Briefing.com analysts, who noted that neither Anthropic's IPO nor Nvidia's strong earnings had restored investor confidence. New York's S&P [q5: 500], which trades shares of major tech companies, shed [q6: 3.7 per cent] on Friday, extending a run of losses; the Nasdaq fell more than five per cent while Asian markets tumbled between five and [q8: 6.2 per cent]. Nvidia slumped by [q7: 14.01 per cent], despite posting profits earlier in the week, amid worries about US restrictions on its chips for Chinese companies and leadership turmoil following Jensen Huang's resignation.
items.title: Anthropic's strong IPO debut failed to calm AI-sector fears as tech stocks fell sharply on Friday (Nov [d1: 20]) amid worries over valuations and capital commitments.

items.summary: The article reports that two men, Michael Donovan and Richard Moore, were fined $811m in 2024 by a federal judge (Elizabeth Dillon) after being found liable for running what the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau called a predatory immigrant-services scam. The firm they co-founded, Libre by Nexus — also known as Nexus, founded in 2013 and at one point described as the largest immigration bail company in America — enabled more than 20,000 migrants to be released on bail over about a decade while taking in more than $230m in revenue. The CFPB lawsuit alleged that the firm trapped clients into paying high, long-term fees and misrepresented or concealed terms such as non-refundable monthly payments; for example, Rosa Murillo was told she would pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case completed, though court documents said Nexus stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018. The judge's judgment also forbade the company from collecting on past debts. Days after that 2024 order, Donovan sold some of the company's assets — including customer lists and records — for $3.50, with the buyer taking on its debt; a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith bought those assets and launched Libre Immigration Services (LIS). The judge later ruled in March that this sale violated her order by transferring the debts and voided it, but did not shut LIS down. A former Nexus paralegal who moved to LIS said the lines between the two companies blurred after the sale; another employee confirmed an app intended to collect debts from old clients was never finished because they could not obtain client data. LIS denies wrongdoing, saying it was never in possession of the client lists and that a sign for its office would be installed pending permits. The article notes that since President Donald Trump returned to office, ICE has made over 1.2m arrests with fast-tracked deportations, increasing demand for bond companies; bail can run upwards of $7,000; and a 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
items.title: Former Nexus co-founders fined $811m for scamming detained migrants; successor company Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit clients and collect fees despite the fine.

visual.alt: Bar chart. Donovan 811 $; took 230 $; Libre Immigration Services 10,000 $.

items.summary: The African National Congress suffered its worst electoral result since taking power in [d1: 1994], winning a majority in just one of nine provinces (Limpopo, down from six) and the most votes in only two of eight cities versus six in [d2: 2021]. Nationally it still topped the vote with [q1: 31%] against its previous [q2: 46%], though nationally that figure sits at [q3: 25%], up from [q4: 22%] five years earlier, while Jacob Zuma's MK Party came third on [q5: 10%] and dominated KwaZulu-Natal with [q6: 34%]. The pro-business Democratic Alliance won the most votes in Gauteng (Johannesburg, Pretoria, Ekurhuleni) but secured an outright majority only in Cape Town. With parties having until 27 November to form local governments, ANC officials—who reportedly view a DA partnership as a last resort—appear set to court smaller parties instead; ActionSA's [q7: 17%] provincial showing makes it a potential kingmaker in Gauteng where the DA and ANC cannot agree on mayoral candidates. Analysts warn that this reluctance signals strain within the Government of National Unity, which has remained intact since forming in [d4: 2024], while noting that past power-sharing arrangements have been unstable and that resolving municipal service failures could take a decade rather than one term.
items.title: ANC's worst local election result in 30 years forces scramble for city power-sharing deals

visual.alt: Bar chart. any other party 31 %; down 46 %.

items.summary: The Victorian Greens applied to the Supreme Court for an urgent injunction against independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan, alleging his campaign distributed how-to-vote cards using the party's colour scheme, font and triangle logo with a banner reading "Vote 1 Green Values" that instructed voters to preference him first followed by Animal Justice Party, another independent, then the Liberals in fourth place. The Greens are contesting Prahran, an ultra-marginal seat they lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection by a margin of 1.3%, and fear Labor's open ticket could deprive them of preference votes. State director Martin Shield requested Finnigan stop distributing the material on Wednesday afternoon, threatening legal action if no undertaking was given within two hours; Finnigan produced an amended card with different colours and a banner reading "Vote 1 Trans Greens Values" that included a disclaimer stating he is not an endorsed Greens candidate. The changes did not satisfy the Greens, whose lawyer Adam McBeth lodged papers on Friday afternoon alleging voters at prepoll were deliberately misled by volunteers wearing greens matching genuine party shirts and standing next to Greens placards. At the initial hearing on Friday night, Justice John Watson said the first card "looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate" but adjourned until 3pm Saturday for VEC testimony; Finnigan argued he was self-represented, lacked funds to print new cards, and chose Irish green because of his background. The Victorian Election Commission accepted the revised card after the action was lodged. This is an ongoing legal dispute with no ruling reported as of the article's writing.
items.title: Victorian Greens sought an urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards that mimicked their branding while preferring the Liberals last.

items.summary: At a Friday White House press briefing ostensibly celebrating his Asia trip, President Trump used the event to test potential successors JD Vance and Marco Rubio for the 2028 election. Emerson College's latest national poll has Rubio ahead of Vance as favourite, though Vance is widely expected to seek the presidency; neither received an answer from Trump when a reporter asked which would make a better president after him. The conference also featured Stephen Miller, recently appointed White House chief of staff, whom Trump praised and then jokingly asked if he wanted to run for president, stirring the succession race further.
items.title: Trump turns White House press conference into a 2028 succession audition

items.summary: Legal experts say the International Court of Justice's ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya could strengthen South Africa's genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza, establishing a precedent that genocidal intent can coexist with a military objective. The two conflicts are legally distinct but share a common basis: both cases allege state breaches of obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention. On Thursday, the court found Myanmar violated the convention on multiple grounds stemming from mistreatment of the Muslim Rohingya minority by the armed forces.
items.title: Myanmar genocide judgment may bolster Gaza case against Israel

items.summary: Honda announced a recall of 810,592 older cars and SUVs in the United States because certain Takata air bag inflators could rupture. The affected vehicles include some 2013 Honda Accords, 2012-2013 Civics, 2012-2013 CR-Vs, and 2013 Acura ILX and RDX models originally sold or registered in 14 states or territories known for high temperature, humidity, and large temperature fluctuations. Honda reported no injuries or crashes tied to the recalled vehicles and no air bag inflator ruptures; however, long-term monitoring revealed potential propellant degradation in specific inflators within those geographic regions. This recall involves inflators containing a moisture-absorbing material, unlike millions of previously recalled vehicles. The Takata issue has prompted at least 28 deaths in the United States since 2009 and triggered more than 100 million vehicle recalls worldwide, including about 67 million in the U.S., across roughly two dozen major automakers over the past decade.
items.title: Honda recalls over 810,000 U.S. vehicles due to Takata air bag rupture risk

items.summary: 70-year-old inmate Reinaldo Dennes was executed by lethal injection in Texas, but the process took more than an hour and he repeatedly reported excruciating pain. He cried out 'The pain! Go!' moments after being strapped to the gurney, described his right leg as a cramping sensation that felt abnormal, and pleaded with God not to let him suffer for 63 minutes before death was pronounced at 7:07pm; he had been sentenced for the 1996 murder of diamond dealer Janos Szucs. TDCJ spokeswoman Amanda Hernandez rejected claims the execution was 'botched', stating IVs were placed in viable veins and that Dennes alleged pain where no IVs existed, though she conceded inmates have made such allegations before; Reverend Jeff Hood, who has witnessed 13 executions by lethal injection, said he had never seen someone able to make complete sentences past 30 seconds. The case adds weight to renewed scrutiny of pentobarbital—the most commonly used execution drug—after Christa Pike survived a botched attempt in September and after a federal review raised concerns about unnecessary pain; the Biden administration has barred its use federally, though states retain discretion. Public support for capital punishment fell to a five-decade low of 52 per cent in late 2025, down from an 80 per cent peak in 1994, with Gallup finding 49 per cent favour the death penalty and 45 per cent oppose it.
items.title: Texas execution of Reinaldo Dennes lasted over an hour amid reports of severe pain

items.summary: The Gold Coast's official schoolies celebrations drew an estimated [q1: 12,000 people] registering in [d1: 2025], continuing a five-year year-on-year decline. Queensland Youth Minister Sam O'Connor said the event had evolved to suit young people's changing tastes, adding more daytime and free activities such as a Ferris wheel, run clubs, line dancing and pickleball. Superintendent Peter Miles reported an increased police presence in Surfers Paradise over the weekend, including drug dogs and mounted officers; [q2: 16 schoolies] were arrested alongside [q3: 66 non-schoolies or 'toolies'] during 2025, with balcony safety also flagged as a concern. Community groups such as Red Frogs described an 'amazing shift' in culture toward daytime activities and reduced early-morning drinking. Griffith Institute of Tourism professor Daniel Gschwind noted that schoolies peaked at up to [q4: 50,000 young] people attending in the early 2000s but remains a key tourism event despite dwindling numbers as many youths now choose other Queensland locations or overseas destinations like Bali and Fiji.
items.title: Gold Coast schoolies attendance fell to about 12,000 in 2025 amid changing youth tastes and safety concerns.

items.summary: CGTN reports that China's new energy vehicle (NEV) exports reached approximately 3 million units during the first seven months of 2026, framing this surge as evidence of Chinese automakers expanding across APEC economies and creating opportunities for local suppliers. The report accompanies a CGTN episode of 'The Win-Win Code' in which host Liu Xin visits XPENG, a Guangzhou-based smart mobility company, to experience its Robotaxi service firsthand and explore the technology behind driverless travel; VP Alex discusses how Chinese smart carmakers are shaping future mobility and addresses public comfort with autonomous vehicles. The export figure is presented as an unverified source claim tied specifically to NEVs in that period rather than total vehicle exports or a confirmed trend, while the XPENG visit serves promotional coverage of the program's guest segment.
items.title: China's new energy vehicle exports reach around 3 million in first seven months of 2026

items.summary: The Win-Win Code's first episode examines how Chinese investment has transformed Kuantan Port in Malaysia into a major logistics hub, framing the project as generating local jobs and fostering professional and cultural exchanges. The program uses this case to explore China's broader economic ties with the Asia-Pacific, posing open questions about what drives regional growth and how trade and supply chains are evolving—questions left unanswered rather than resolved. Guests include Ben Ye of Beibu Gulf Holding (Malaysia), Prof. Qian Jun of Fudan University's International School of Finance, and Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies. The episode is presented as promotional content inviting viewers to join the series; no specific figures or outcomes are reported.
items.title: Kuantan Port: Chinese investment reshaping a Malaysian logistics hub

items.summary: A magnitude 6.9 earthquake occurred approximately 22 kilometers (14 miles) west-northwest of Ondores in central Peru's Junin region, according to the US Geological Survey. The quake happened at 7:09 pm local time on Friday and reached a depth of about 142.1 km (88 mi). The US National Tsunami Warning Center reported no tsunami warning, advisory, watch or threat following the event, and there were no immediate reports of casualties or significant damage.
items.title: Magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck Peru's Junin region

items.summary: The UN expressed concern over reported Saudi-led coalition airstrikes on Yemen's Port of Hudaydah, warning that escalating hostilities in Sanaa, Saada, and Taiz threaten civilians, critical infrastructure, and vital supply routes for millions. Deputy spokesman Farhan Haq said the world body is closely monitoring reports of strikes on the Red Sea port as well as ongoing military operations across those governorates. He stressed the need to safeguard continuity of Yemen's Red Sea ports, which serve as a lifeline to millions, and called on all parties to comply with international humanitarian law, including prohibitions on attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure. Haq reiterated that there is no military solution to the conflict and urged all parties to return to political negotiations. The Saudi-led coalition announced Friday it had launched an operation against Houthi facilities allegedly used in attacks on civilians in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
items.title: UN warns Saudi-led strikes on Port of Hudaydah threaten aid lifeline

items.summary: The Los Angeles County Fire Department's Air Operations team rescued a woman from a flood control channel in City of Industry, California, on Friday. Footage shows the department's helicopter crew locating her before lowering a paramedic into the channel; the paramedic secured the woman to a rescue winch and both were lifted out and brought safely to the ground. The account is based on video footage rather than an official statement from the department.
items.title: Helicopter rescue of woman trapped in City of Industry flood channel

items.summary: The 'World This Week' episode, presented by Gavin Lee and produced by Alessandro Xenos, Théophile Vareille, Juliette Laffont and Laura Burloux, frames three events as historic. The first is President Trump's three-way summit in China with Presidents Xi and Putin, which hosts describe as unprecedented; the program assesses its choreography and consequences without attributing specific outcomes. A second milestone was Myanmar becoming the first state ever found to have committed genocide by an ICJ ruling. A third development was Britain resetting its relations with the EU, raising whether it should 'Bre-join' the bloc. The panel of four foreign correspondents offered analysis across these topics; no quantitative data or specific claims about consequences were reported in the item.
items.title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit in China; ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar; Britain's reset with the EU

items.summary: Indigenous T’boli farmers near Lake Sebu, Philippines, suspected that switching from organic to glyphosate-tolerant genetically modified (GM) corn accelerated soil erosion and siltation killing fish in the lake. With support from MASIPAG scientists, they tested two plots—one with traditional white corn grown organically, one with GM corn treated with glyphosate—measuring erosion over a cropping season from March to July 2025. They found that conventional farms lost [q14: 39 m]3 of soil per hectare ([q15: 557.4 ft]3 per acre), more than five times the traditional plot’s loss of [q12: 7.59 cubic] meters per hectare ([q13: 108.5 cubic] feet per acre). An independent expert attributed this to glyphosate killing all vegetation except GM corn, removing root cover on steep slopes and leaving soil vulnerable to gravity-driven erosion; the herbicide also persists in soils for up to six months after use. Researchers noted that most such studies examine flat U.S. fields, not mountainous Philippine terrain where topsoil loss is more severe. Farmers reported higher input costs—[q18: 1,500 pesos] per sack ([q19: $23.5] per sack) of GM corn seeds alone—and financial risks from climate shocks; one family lost [q27: 10,000]-[q28: 15,000 pesos] ([q29: $157]-[q30: $235]) in a season. The farmers hope the results support lobbying for local ordinances banning glyphosate in riparian zones.
items.title: T’boli farmers in Mindanao found glyphosate corn caused far more soil erosion than traditional farming

items.summary: The op-ed argues that maps of Central African states are used by foreign interests and elites as tools to perpetuate power over natural resources, which tend to flow outwards rather than benefiting local populations. The Congo Basin is described as a patchwork of extractive concessions, protected areas, and carbon offset projects that have failed to stem deforestation while causing human rights and food security impacts. Only around [q1: 5%] of the forest is currently under formal community tenure or management rights, significantly less than the estimated [q2: 35%] under Indigenous title in the Amazon despite higher population density there. The authors attribute this gap to ill-adapted legal frameworks (Gabon and Cameroon) or no enforceable legislation at all (Central African Republic and Republic of Congo). They call for governments and donors to accelerate community land tenure reforms, citing the DRC's November COP commitment to place more than [q3: 50 million hectares] (over [q4: 123 million acres]) under IPLC control—a tenfold increase—and draft legislation in CAR, Gabon, and Cameroon. The authors stress that laws are only powerful if enforceable, so they urge scaling up participatory mapping tools to let communities demonstrate their presence for recognition by policymakers and the private sector.
items.title: Congo Basin forest communities lack formal land rights; mapping and legal reform urged to secure tenure

items.summary: Ahead of their opening match against Venezuela, Cameroon's Under-17 team are described as confident and mentally ready by the coach, who said all players were 'OK' and expressed pride in the squad's confidence. Players acknowledge a tough contest but remain determined to secure their first win and progress beyond the group stage; one player characterized Venezuela as a serious challenge while another cited ambitions of reaching far in the tournament. A player also voiced an aspirational claim that Africa can win the World Cup, framing it as placing Cameroon at the top of world football—though this is presented as ambition rather than established fact.
items.title: Cameroon U17s seek opening win over Venezuela at FIFA U-17 World Cup

items.summary: A Funcas think tank report based on Eurostat and Spain's National Institute of Statistics data finds that severe material and social deprivation affected [q3: 8.1%] of the Spanish population in [d2: 2025], after peaking in [d3: 2023]. This compares to a EU figure of [q4: 6.3%], which fell over the same period, while Spain's rate rose from [q1: 7.4%] in [d1: 2015] when it compared favorably at [q2: 9.7%]. The ranking shift is partly methodological: Eurostat replaced a measure based on four out of nine hardship indicators with one requiring seven out of thirteen, adding items like not being able to buy new clothes or meet friends. Poverty disproportionately affects minors below age [q12: 16] at almost [q11: 11%], single-parent households (over [q14: 80%] run by women), and working-age people aged 30-64, whose rate reached almost [q15: 9%]. The over-65 demographic falls below [q16: 5%], attributed to stable pensions and home ownership. Rising rents—up over [q7: 10%] year-on-year—are a key driver; per a BBVA Foundation and Ivie study, [q8: 20%] of lowest-income households spend on average [q9: 57.4%] of income on rent versus the recommended [q10: 30%]. Social organizations argue that growth and employment have not eradicated poverty, noting more than [q6: 30%] of people in severe poverty actually work, and call for direct transfers rather than tax deductions inaccessible to low-income households.
items.title: Spain's severe material and social deprivation rose to 8.1% in 2025 despite GDP growth, edging past the EU average as it slipped from fifteenth to fifth among member states.

items.summary: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Azerbaijan and Armenia to advance projects he calls "of strategic importance to Europe both economically and politically," framing the region amid Russia's war on Ukraine as a source of diversification for reliable partners. Berlin prioritizes moving forward the Middle Corridor transport network linking Asia and Europe through the South Caucasus, which Wadephul described as strategically important during regional destabilization; Azerbaijan's Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov acknowledged that implementing the 42-kilometre corridor route through Armenian territory would be difficult without cooperation with Armenia. Germany seeks a signed peace agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia to underpin security and stability, which it treats as both a diplomatic objective and European strategic interest.
items.title: Germany steps up engagement with South Caucasus as 'region of opportunities',

items.summary: Morocco defeated Fiji 6-0 in the opening match of the FIFA U-17 World Cup, moving to the top of Group H. Coach Hichem Ben Labsir attributed the result to his players' preparation and teamwork rather than individual effort, while a player described the first match as crucial and called the 6-0 scoreline good. The victory gives Morocco an early advantage heading into their remaining group matches.
items.title: Morocco opened their FIFA U-17 World Cup campaign with a 6-0 win over Fiji to top Group H.

items.summary: Spain's Audiencia Nacional provisionally released James Cox Chambers, known as Fergie, after the United States acknowledged three "substantial errors" in translating its extradition documents. The U.S. admitted it added the word "violence," which did not appear in the original text, while distancing itself from the translation contractor and calling the mistakes unintentional and an isolated case. However, Chambers' lawyers argued there were actually thirty such changes showing deliberate alteration to portray him as violent; his attorney Aitor Martínez claimed Washington manipulated a sworn FBI statement and tied the charges to President Trump's September 25, 2025 National Security Memorandum directing cases against left-wing groups. The court imposed precautionary measures—withdrawn passport, barred from leaving Spain, weekly court appearances—and signed by three judges of the Criminal Chamber concluded that these errors challenge the extradition request itself and may affect its final outcome. Chambers faces up to 30 years in U.S. prison for allegedly terrorist activities stemming from pro-Palestinian activism; his wife Stella Schnabel said he is suffering political persecution, though this remains an assertion rather than a court finding.
items.title: Spanish court releases pro-Palestinian billionaire Fergie Chambers over US translation errors

items.summary: The US government asserts that restrictions on Chinese firms accessing Nvidia's technology remain intact, even as scrutiny intensifies over the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and AMD to companies located or headquartered in China. Commerce Secretary Bessent told CNBC that 'the proper chip restrictions are in place' and 'the remote access has been curtailed,' a claim made after returning from an Asia trip with President Trump. The comments followed the House Foreign Affairs Committee's release of details on the Commerce Department approving those sales, some to companies the Pentagon identified as having ties to the Chinese military. Nvidia reported that it stopped shipping its H200 chips to China earlier in the week despite prior approvals; a spokesperson said 'the limited shipments we made under the H200 programme were legal and authorised,' with a review process spanning more than half a year, while AMD stated it complies with US export control laws. The controversy centers on Megaspeed International, which uses advanced chips to provide computing power that Chinese firms access remotely; Bessent said he was frustrated by the Commerce Department's delay in placing controls on Megaspeed and publicly rebuked his colleague over jurisdiction, though Trump said he has 'not lost confidence' in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The article frames these statements as government assertions rather than independently verified outcomes, noting that Chinese firms are bracing for impacts on their AI development plans as scrutiny mounts.
items.title: US says Nvidia chip export curbs are in place amid scrutiny over China access

items.summary: Hair Anatomy founder Dominique Bogle left corporate banking eight months after going live on TikTok from her kitchen in [d1: 2022], building the business to nearly £15,000 of monthly wig sales. She started selling through her website with Instagram traffic and initially dismissed TikTok as a dancing app before changing her mind in [d4: 2022]. Her live sessions split into morning packing lives showing orders being wrapped and evening show-and-tell sessions demonstrating wigs, totaling at least four hours per day; she also shares openly about her own alopecia to build personal connection. By [d5: 2025], the Birmingham founder had 60,000 TikTok followers while shipping across continents. The model relies on social commerce expected to surpass $100 billion in [d9: 2026] and account for more than [q7: 8 per cent] of total e-commerce sales, with beauty capturing over half; Bogle says authenticity sells rather than polished aesthetics.
items.title: UK banker Dominique Bogle quit finance after TikTok wig sales reached almost £15,000 in one month.

items.summary: The Congress party characterized Prime Minister Narendra Modi's speech to Ficci lamenting stagnant wages, jobs, and growing economic disparity as an admission that his own government is responsible for the problem. Rahul Gandhi accused Modi of creating monopolies by handing ports, airports, coal, roads, power, mines, and jungles to specific groups, arguing these monopolies drive up prices and eliminate competition rather than create jobs; he blamed demonetisation and GST for destroying small traders and MSMEs while wiping out honest competitors. Congress spokesperson Jairam Ramesh argued that Modi's manifesto in the 2024 Lok Sabha election stated exactly what he told Ficci, but then labeled Congress as driven by an 'urban naxal mindset against wealth creators.' He attributed the lack of private investment—which he said is necessary for wage and job growth—to Modi's policies. Ramesh also cited that imports from China this year will touch a record $150 billion, up from $112 billion, which he claims has decimated MSMEs, and accused Modi of misusing enforcement agencies to benefit select corporates while claiming GDP growth figures appear only in headlines.
items.title: Congress frames PM Modi's Ficci remarks on jobs and wages as a confession of his policies' failures

items.summary: At The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, Palmer Luckey argued that Beijing benefits from Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO and called for his return. His reasoning rests on a distinction between Chinese AI companies—which want to buy Nvidia chips—and the Chinese government, which prefers domestic processors; per Luckey, 600,000 H200 GPUs are reportedly sitting in a port denied an import permit because Beijing wants its own silicon industry rather than one dependent on the United States. He acknowledged disagreeing with Huang over chip exports to China and conceded those were reasonable arguments others share, dismissing critics who call his stance ‘the midwit take.’ Luckey framed Huang’s ouster as serving Chinese interests while weakening America, citing a trillion dollars knocked off Nvidia’s market cap, and asserted that interim CEO Lisa Su is not the right person for such a critical juncture because she did not build the company from scratch. The article also reports his personal remark that Huang ‘shouldn’t have slept with whatever she turns out to be,’ referring to the woman named as interim CEO.
items.title: Palmer Luckey says China wants Jensen Huang out, so he wants him back

items.summary: The three major US indexes closed lower, with the Nasdaq Composite plunging [q6: 5.13%] to lead the rout while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell [q8: 1.85%]. The S&P 500 dropped [q2: 257.38 points], or [q3: 3.59%], and both it and the Dow ended more than [q11: 10%] below their record closing highs, confirming corrections; the Nasdaq erased its year-to-date gains as investors retreated from technology and AI-linked stocks despite strong corporate earnings. The S&P 500 fell for a seventh consecutive session, marking its longest losing streak since February [d2: 2020]. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said the central bank’s policy rate was not sufficiently high to address elevated inflation, while traders were pricing in a near-certain [q15: 25]-basis-point interest-rate increase at the Fed’s December meeting. Anthropic shares closed [q13: 17.1%] above their [q14: $83] offer price on Thursday but surrendered much of that gain, and Bitcoin fell below [q17: $60,000].
items.title: US stocks fell sharply on a weak AI trade and tariff fears; S&P 500 entered correction.

visual.alt: Bar chart. plunged 1,225.05 point; Dow 908.88 point.

items.summary: Google announced Thursday that its Gemini assistant can now take control of a user's Mac to perform tasks such as clicking, typing, navigating menus, and filling forms—examples include color-grading photos in preferred software and preparing clothing images for resale listings. The capability is available immediately for US users with the Mac Gemini app who hold Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscriptions. Alongside OpenAI's ChatGPT and Meta's Muse, which already offer similar computer-use features on their Mac software, this positions Gemini among established agents that act beyond question-and-answer chatbots. When active, Gemini operates in an isolated background window while users retain control of the main screen and cursor; Google states consumers can choose which apps are accessible, watch each step live, pause at any time, and approve key actions beforehand. The move intensifies pressure on Apple to enhance Siri, whose current capabilities cover tasks within its own apps—such as sending iMessages or adding calendar events—but not most third-party software, though Apple has begun releasing frameworks that could let developers extend such abilities. Separately, Apple has pledged new Mac privacy controls after warning of rising risks from granting AI software broad data access.
items.title: Google's Gemini gains 'computer use' for Macs, matching ChatGPT and Muse

items.summary: A TCS employee, Manish Yadav, alleges that management denied him entry to the Adibatla campus while he wore traditional attire for Ayyappa Deeksha, which he said he had informed them about two months in advance. He questioned why colleagues were permitted similar dress and named senior colleague Sikender Shah as a discriminator. Following his account, Ayyappa devotees and Hindu organisations gathered outside the campus on Thursday to protest and demand that Manish be allowed to work; BJP leader Andela Sriramulu Yadav joined the demonstration demanding action against those responsible. Adibatla police intervened when protesters attempted entry, described the incident as a misunderstanding over dress code rather than communal, ruled out any communal angle, stated they had received no formal complaint, and reported that TCS has issued no official statement on the allegations.
items.title: TCS Adibatla Employee Alleges Denial of Entry Over Religious Attire

items.summary: The University Grants Commission (UGC) issued a public advisory warning students and parents against enrolling in unrecognised institutions. Its official list of fake universities has grown from [q1: 20] to [q2: 32] over the past three years. Notably, [q3: 18] of the [q4: 20 institutions] flagged as early as March [d1: 2023] remain on the current list despite repeated warnings and letters urging state governments to take action.
items.title: UGC's fake-university list grew from 20 to 32 in three years, with most earlier names retained

items.summary: The rupee weakened to a record low of around ₹96 in March [q1], then climbed to ₹93.63, its best level in six months [q2]. This rebound is attributed to double-digit export growth for six straight months and foreign investors buying nearly $6 billion worth of Indian equities in just 10 days of November [q3], after pulling out over $30 billion earlier this year [q4]. The RBI also stepped in directly with different schemes. However, the text poses an open question—whether the RBI truly stabilised the rupee or only bought time while underlying pressures remain—rather than asserting a conclusion.
items.title: Rupee's recovery bonanza: RBI stabilisation questioned amid mixed signals

items.summary: Cyclone Avkan made landfall near Gopalpur on the Odisha coast as a cyclonic storm with wind speeds of 70-80 kmph and gusts up to 90 kmph before weakening into a depression, according to IMD Director General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra. The system moved northwards at 12 kmph in the six hours leading up to 5.30 pm on Friday and was centred around 70 km south-southwest of Angul when assessed; it is expected to weaken further into a low-pressure area over the next six hours, with rainfall intensity declining from Saturday. Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari reported no major damage or loss of life despite heavy rainfall across several districts. The Odisha government announced three-day school holidays (Thursday-Saturday) for government, aided and private schools in nine districts initially, later extended to 13 total; however, the Saturday closure applies only to six districts—Ganjam, Gajapati, Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapara and Kandhamal. District collectors were asked to assess local conditions for additional closures. In Tamil Nadu, schools remained open on Friday in Chennai as no statewide holiday was declared; similarly, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and Andhra Pradesh announced no statewide holidays, with the arrangement expected to continue unless district authorities issue separate orders. The government moved more than 4.40 lakh people to safer locations after ruling out an immediate flood threat.
items.title: Cyclone Avkan weakened into a depression after landfall near Gopalpur, Odisha; school closures limited to six districts on Saturday

items.summary: Despite a reported US-Iran war that closed the Strait of Hormuz, petrol and diesel retail prices stayed largely unchanged in New Delhi (₹102.12/₹95.20), Mumbai (₹111.21/₹97.83), Chennai (₹107.76/₹99.55), Kolkata (₹113.51/₹99.82), Bengaluru (₹110.44/₹99.56) and Hyderabad (₹116.15/₹104.23). Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri attributed the stability to a ₹10-per-litre cut in central excise duty on both fuels, while noting that global crude hovered around $92 per barrel versus roughly $67-68 pre-disruption and rose 50-60% in several countries. India's October crude imports rose ~4.7% month-on-month to 23.31 million metric tons (up ~11% year-on-year from 21 million tons), oil-product imports fell 2.8% monthly but down ~41% annually, product exports rose 4.7% to 5.36 million tons, and fuel consumption climbed nearly 10% month-on-month to 20.49 million metric tons—its highest since March.
items.title: Petrol and diesel prices remained steady across major Indian cities on November 21 despite a global crude surge

items.summary: The provided text is a quiz titled 'Question Time' from what appears to be a weekly news program, but it contains no substantive content—only an orientation notice stating that landscape mode is unsupported and instructing viewers to return to portrait mode. No questions, answers, figures, or claims are present in the source material.
items.title: Weekly News Quiz: Question Time

items.summary: Pakistani minister Musadik Malik, making his first visit to India in more than three years, told reporters on Friday that Pakistan would fully support efforts to advance regional peace and security while stressing the forum focused on multilateral issues. Speaking at the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum hosted by India at Purana Qila, Malik emphasised culture's role in building bridges between countries, saying mutual understanding is essential for progress. He declined to comment on bilateral matters including cross-border terrorism, noting even India had not raised such topics and that substantive talks would follow once the forum concluded. Malik referenced reports he was denied permission to visit sites like the Taj Mahal but said his programme there remained unfinalised pending the event's conclusion. The Congress party criticised the BJP-led government for inviting Pakistan amid ongoing concerns about terrorism sponsorship, with spokesperson Supriya Shrinate questioning why India welcomed Pakistani representatives while Pakistan allegedly continued sponsoring terror attacks.
items.title: Pakistan minister Malik stresses culture's role in dialogue at SCO forum

items.summary: Karnataka Assembly Leader of the Opposition and BJP figure R Ashoka warned in Mangaluru that the BJP would firmly resist any move by Chief Minister DK Shivakumar's Congress-led government to amend or repeal Karnataka's anti-conversion and anti-cow slaughter laws. The warning followed a statement by Congress MLC Ivan D'Souza about intentions to amend religious conversion law, which Ashoka framed as minority appeasement. Both laws were introduced during the previous BJP dispensation: the Prevention of Slaughter and Preservation of Cattle Act was passed in December 2020 and notified February 2021 under Basavaraj Bommai (with a prior attempt withdrawn by Congress in 2013), while the Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Bill was tabled during BS Yeddiyurappa's tenure, brought into force via ordinance in May 2022 before legislative passage in September 2022. Ashoka chose Mangaluru—an RSS stronghold in coastal Karnataka—deliberately, as Congress held its first Cabinet meeting outside Bengaluru there on September 18 to signal outreach toward a region where BJP has long enjoyed an electoral advantage while Congress struggled for decades. The warning reframes the ideological contest ahead of the 2028 Assembly elections, raising whether Shivakumar's coastal push will yield gains or hand the Opposition another chance to consolidate its traditional support base; this remains a forecast rather than an outcome.
items.title: BJP leader warns Congress government against repealing anti-conversion and anti-cow slaughter laws

items.summary: The West Bengal Chief Electoral Officer unilaterally postponed the state's scheduled November 23 start of the special summary revision (SSR) of its photo-electoral roll, citing "unavoidable circumstances" without giving a reason. The delay is widely attributed to slow disposal of pending Supreme Court and Appellate Tribunal appeals from the controversial special intensive revision (SIR), which had dropped voters before summer assembly elections; ECI officials said they did not know why Bengal postponed it but noted only the poll panel can approve any revised schedule, so the January 16 final roll would remain largely intact. The postponement leaves new and first-time voters—especially those turning 18 by [d1: January 1, 2027]—without a clear registration date or draft list to check, while millions of SIR deletion appeals stay pending; ECI reported last month that around [q5: 126,194 applications] were disposed of out of roughly [q4: 3.8 million appeals], and Bengal's tribunals had rejected about [q17: 2.7 million people].
items.title: West Bengal's special summary voter roll revision postponed amid unresolved SIR appeals

items.summary: The inaugural Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians conference in Bengaluru (November 17-18) was criticized for sidelining substantive debates on representation, with men dominating both the promotional posters and the dais. India has just [q1: 74] women parliamentarians under [q2: 14%] in the Lok Sabha and about [q3: 39] in the Rajya Sabha, forcing a [q4: 150]-strong audience to be filled with MLCs/MLAs and foreign delegates. Vocal women MPs were absent from the event; posters featured seven men (including the Lok Sabha Speaker, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, Karnataka CM) versus just two women. The article attributes male gatekeeping as the mechanism behind this sidelining, noting that well-clad women politicians received platitudes rather than substantive engagement on issues like cyber-stalking and delinking reservations from delimitation.
items.title: Bengaluru CWP meet sidelined women's voices amid male gatekeeping

items.summary: At a November 20, 2026 meeting with Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis to review the state's development projects, NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri urged Maharashtra to adopt an ambitious long-term land acquisition policy and acquire land in advance for future projects. Lahiri argued that land available at lower prices today could become more valuable over time, so early acquisition would let proper management generate substantial revenue while keeping the interests of future generations in mind; he also called for resolving pending issues related to land acquisition, infrastructure, and agriculture on priority. Fadnavis said his government was focusing on long-term planning, proper land management, timely implementation of infrastructure projects, and increasing agricultural productivity, thanking NITI Aayog for its guidance while expressing hope it would continue supporting the state's development efforts. Lahiri also expressed satisfaction with progress on Maharashtra's Vadhavan port project; senior officials from various state departments along with representatives from the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority, Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority, and Maharashtra Maritime Board attended the meeting.
items.title: NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman Urges Maharashtra To Acquire Land In Advance For Future Projects

items.summary: The Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar memorial at Indu Mill in Mumbai faces a further delay, with statue construction stalled for six months as the state government has not cleared a contractor's proposal seeking an additional Rs [q1: 350 crore]. The escalation is attributed to rising copper and bronze prices linked to West Asian geopolitical tensions. Structural work on supporting buildings—library, auditorium, museum—is nearly [q2: 95 per cent] complete, but statue-related suspension remains the main hurdle. Projected costs rose from an initial contract of around Rs [q3: 763 crore] to Rs [q4: 783 crore] in [d2: 2018], then to around Rs [q5: 1,089 crore], and are now expected to cross Rs [q6: 1,200 crore]. The statue's design was revised upward from a proposed height of [q7: 250 feet] to [q8: 350 feet] with a [q9: 100]-foot pedestal, bringing total height to [q10: 450 feet]. Opposition leaders condemned the delay; Anand Raj Ambedkar alleged deliberate stalling and questioned fund handling, while Harshwardhan Sapkal accused the government of playing divide-and-rule. The project's history spans demand between [d3: 2007] and [d4: 2011], in-principle approval for allotting [q11: 12 acres] in December [d5: 2012], a land transfer agreement signed April [d6: 2015], a groundbreaking on [d7: October 11, 2015], and contract award in [d8: 2018]. The delay is framed as reflecting broader government financial strain from schemes such as Ladki Bahin. All cost figures are reported estimates; the ₹350 crore proposal remains pending rather than approved.
items.title: Indu Mill Ambedkar Memorial Faces Two-Year Delay Over Pending ₹350-Crore Cost Escalation Proposal

items.summary: US President Donald Trump announced Friday that the United States would penalize American companies constructing data centers overseas, stating he would impose a "tremendous tax" on such facilities. The statement was made while discussing AI at a White House news conference following his trip to Asia, with Trump declaring, "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country." Data centers are considered critical to the AI boom because they provide the computing power needed to train and run increasingly complex AI systems. The proposed penalty could complicate the global AI buildout; developers often locate facilities close to users to reduce delays for time-sensitive tasks such as payment processing, and transmitting large volumes of data over long distances can add significant costs.
items.title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on US companies building data centres abroad

items.summary: Encrypted messaging service Signal announced on Friday that it would restrict screenshot access by default, warning that embedding agentic AI in consumer devices is an existential threat to its privacy mission. The measure reflects growing tension between privacy-focused apps and the biggest tech companies racing to roll out screen-reading agents; Signal identified Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence as particularly worrisome due to their deep OS integration, while noting it previously blocked Microsoft's Recall on Windows but could not reliably offer such protections on macOS. The service described its new protections as "incomplete" and urged operating system providers—Apple, Alphabet's Google, and Microsoft—to give developers more concrete ways to block agents from accessing sensitive data and provide information about how their agents function so systems can be adjusted accordingly. Signal said that AI systems scanning screens undermine end-to-end encryption by pulling messages out of its secure environment into other servers; it also cited Reuters reporting that Meta's Muse agent bypassed its own Connector tool on both Apple and Android, using OS-level permissions including accessibility tools to extract text from screenshots. An Apple update this week closed the specific pathway but introduced new agent permissions with additional user warnings. Signal called for straightforward ways of opting apps out entirely of screen reading, notifications, and other file system access by AI assistants; it is owned by a non-profit foundation that limits stored data, eschews ads, and cannot read conversations itself. Apple, Google, and Microsoft did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
items.title: Signal blocks screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats

items.summary: Artist Sonia Mehra Chawla's solo show Emerald Leaf & Golden Fibre at Gallery Espace, New Friends Colony, New Delhi (on view until November 28), uses historical herbarium sheets and mill photographs to give names to people erased by colonial record-keeping. The exhibition is built on a Plants on Paper fellowship under the Getty's Paper Project Initiative with the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, alongside archives at the University of Dundee; it draws from Francis Buchanan-Hamilton's 1809 Barisal herbarium sheet and works including The Golden Fibre triptych (worked on since 2024), Paat (Jute): The Labouring Body video, Weighing Jute photograph, 'Living' Entities & 'Lively' Gardens pieces, Ancestors III: The Mountain in Their Eyes portraits of six Darjeeling tea-garden women credited by name, and Two Leaves and a Bud videos. A central contrast is drawn between the single named collector on the 1809 Barisal sheet versus the 17 names carried on the label for Two Leaves and a Bud (tea pluckers and sorters of Makaibari). The show also connects jute's history in Bengal to sisal in Tanzania, where estates were taken over by the state from 1967 and families moved into Ujamaa collective villages from 1973. A reported figure places a tea worker in the Bengal gardens at about Rs 250 a day, while the Indian Jute Mills Association warned last December that more than half of West Bengal's mills could shut by March with over two lakh workers.
items.title: Sonia Mehra Chawla's exhibition reclaims colonial botany and jute labour in New Delhi
